Adds the domain (stress group of 1-4 syllables, one primary stress), the phonemic status, the exception class (words ending in particular vowel sequences), and the syllable-count conventions (long vowel = two syllables; unstressed i/u = glides) that make the penult rule hold. new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per stress group of one to four syllables; stress is phonemic but falls on the penultimate syllable in the default case. The only exceptions are certain words ending in particular vowel sequences. Long vowels count as two syllables (VV), and unstressed prevocalic/intervocalic i, u are treated as glides, both analyses chosen so that the penultimate pattern has the fewest exceptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (only one primary stress per stress group).
new_statements.exceptions: Certain words that end in particular vowel sequences (Priest 1968 p. 102, as summarised by SPA); Priest calls stress phonemic, so a residual lexical component exists.
new_statements.identity_note: The SPA entry (and Priest 1968 behind it) describes the Sirionó of eastern Bolivia between the Mamoré and Blanco rivers (Beni), from Priest's fieldwork 1957-1965; no sub-dialect is named. Both listed Priest works are by the same fieldworker on the same variety.

new_statements.quote: 1. EL ACENTO. El conjunto de sílabas sobre el que recae un acento primario, es decir el grupo acentuado, consiste en una secuencia desde una hasta cuatro sílabas. La acentuación es fonémica, aunque por lo general, ocurre en la penúltima sílaba. Las únicas variaciones del patrón predominante son ciertas palabras (no todas) que terminan en las secuencias vocálicas: ei, [...], oi, [...] [list of oral/nasal Vi sequences, scanned-garbled]. Compare por ejemplo, erókoi cola, y erokói pulpa, la parte comestible de la fruta; étei amargo y teréi un pez. En este tratado se lo escribe sólo cuando difiere del patrón predominante, o cuando está ejemplificado, como en esta sección. [§3.3, p. 12:] Se ha interpretado cada vocal larga como dos fonemas homorgánicos porque hay frecuentes agrupaciones de vocales en el lenguaje sirionó, y esta interpretación coincide mejor con el patrón predominante de acentuación: erake [...] pluma; eraake [...] muerto
new_statements.translation: 1. Stress. The set of syllables over which one primary stress falls, i.e. the stress group, consists of a sequence of one to four syllables. Stress is phonemic, although in general it falls on the penultimate syllable. The only departures from the predominant pattern are certain words (not all) that end in the vowel sequences ei, ..., oi, ... Compare e.g. erókoi 'tail' and erokói 'pulp, the edible part of the fruit'; étei 'bitter' and teréi 'a fish'. In this study it is written only when it departs from the predominant pattern, or when exemplified, as in this section. [§3.3:] Each long vowel has been interpreted as two like phonemes because vowel clusters are frequent in Sirionó and this interpretation agrees best with the predominant stress pattern: erake 'feather'; eraake 'dead'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per stress group (1-4 syllables); stress is called phonemic but as a rule falls on the penultimate syllable and is written only where it departs from that; long vowels count as two vowels (two syllables, syllable = V or CV), which keeps forms like eraáke 'dead' penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none described (only one primary stress per stress group is mentioned)
new_statements.exceptions: some (not all) words ending in the vowel sequences ei / oi and their nasal counterparts carry stress off the penult, giving minimal-like pairs erókoi 'cola' vs erokói 'pulpa', étei 'amargo' vs teréi 'un pez'; glides [i̯ u̯] are analysed as /y w/ intervocalically and word-initially when unstressed so as to minimise exceptions to the penult pattern (§3.3, p. 11-12).
new_statements.identity_note: Sirionó (Tupí-Guaraní), as spoken on the río Blanco, Beni/Santa Cruz, Bolivia; Priest's data collected 1957-1965 (c. 600 speakers then). No dialect split is made in the source.

new_statements.quote: 5.1.1. Variaciones de acento. Las enclíticas no acentuadas que no modifican la acentuación de la palabra anterior son: funciones; nominalizador 2 he (3.1.1); nominalizador 3 hi (3.1.); partícula 6 čõ Cualitativa (3.1.1); partícula 4 rã Identificación (3.3.1). Las enclíticas no acentuadas que modifican la acentuación de la palabra anterior son: partícula 7 [čɨ̃] Indicador de interés (3.1.1); partícula 8 sa Indicador de locación (3.1.1); partícula 9 te Enfático (3.1.1, 3.2.1, 3.3.1); partícula 10 alomorfo Yã Negativo (3.1.1, 3.2.1, 5.3); temporal 4 re; nominalizador 1 sa (3.1.1). Cada una de estas enclíticas foneticamente se funde con la palabra precedente quedando el acento en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra fonética. [sec. 1.3, p. 286:] El tercer tono de la secuencia es el tono de la última sílaba acentuada dentro de la oración; ésta puede ser cualquiera de las cinco últimas sílabas de la oración.
new_statements.translation: 5.1.1. Stress variations. The unstressed enclitics that do not modify the stress of the preceding word are: the function markers; nominalizer 2 he; nominalizer 3 hi; particle 6 čõ 'qualitative'; particle 4 rã 'identification'. The unstressed enclitics that DO modify the stress of the preceding word are: particle 7 'concern indicator'; particle 8 sa 'location indicator'; particle 9 te 'emphatic'; particle 10, allomorph Yã, 'negative'; temporal 4 re; nominalizer 1 sa. Each of these enclitics fuses phonetically with the preceding word, the stress remaining on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word. [sec. 1.3:] The third pitch of the sequence is the pitch of the last stressed syllable in the sentence; this may be any of the last five syllables of the sentence.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed-strict penult record (Gasparini 2012) and with the Priest 1968/1980 statement held by the project ('usually on the penultimate syllable'); adds the DOMAIN detail: penultimate stress is computed over the phonological word including the stress-shifting enclitics čɨ̃/sa/te/Yã/re/sa, while he/hi/čõ/rã and the function enclitics stay outside it (word keeps its stress, so surface stress can then be antepenultimate or earlier counting the clitic). Same content as sec. 5.1.1 'Stress variations' of the English Priest & Priest 1967 (BIG II p. 246) already read held by the project; no contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar (a tagmemic morphosyntax with no phonology chapter) presupposes penultimate word stress: one class of unstressed enclitics attaches outside the stress domain (the host keeps its own stress), the other class (čɨ̃, sa, te, Yã, re, nominalizer sa) is incorporated into the phonological word and stress is recomputed so that it again falls on the penultimate syllable of the enlarged phonological word. Since the sentence-final stressed syllable may be any of the last five syllables, the penult of the phonological word can be followed by up to three extrametrical enclitic syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated as such; the only 'variation' is the two-way behaviour of enclitics (stress-neutral he, hi, čõ, rã and the function markers vs stress-shifting čɨ̃, sa, te, Yã, re, sa). The lexical Vi-final exceptions (erókoi vs erokói) of Priest 1968/1980 are not discussed in this chapter.
new_statements.identity_note: Sirionó (Tupí-Guaraní), as spoken on the río Blanco, Beni/Santa Cruz, Bolivia; Priest's data collected 1957-1965 (c. 600 speakers then). No dialect split is made in the source.
